content:
# Workshop 3
 
 # Designing Smarter Engagement with AI
 
 **Speakers:** [Beth Simone Noveck](https:/thegovlab.org/beth-simone-noveck.html) (Founder of InnovateUS and Chief AI Strategist, New Jersey) and [Dane Gambrell](https:/www.linkedin.com/in/dane-gambrell-502091169) (Research Fellow, The GovLab)
 
 This session presents nine questions to consider for designing effective citizen engagement. The checklist emerged from a collaboration with Nesta (the UK's innovation foundation), where Noveck and Gambrell studied 30 global case studies of successful engagement. "Successful" meant engagement that connected to impact and that had been repeated over time.
 
 Noveck opens by noting that even highly successful models like Ireland's Citizens Assembly (which led to referenda on same-sex marriage and abortion) have only been used six times in fifteen years. Singapore tried citizen juries four times and stopped. Engagement remains "tokenistic, occasional, or very small." The goal here is to accelerate, improve, and institutionalize engagement by connecting participation to decision-making and action. If used responsibly, AI offers great opportunities to strengthen engagement.
 
 ## Nine questions
 
 ### 
 
 ### (1) Have you articulated the project’s goals?
 
 The first step is to define why you are conducting the engagement and what you will do with the input. Noveck observes that engagement too often happens "because they have to, not because they need to." There is pressure to be seen consulting the public without clarity on the actual question or how answers will be used.
 
 Example: [New Jersey's AI Task Force used the open-source tool All Our Ideas](https:/rebootdemocracy.ai/blog/new-jersey-ai-task-force-policy-recommendations) [to engage public servants and stakeholders.](https:/rebootdemocracy.ai/blog/new-jersey-ai-task-force-policy-recommendations) Before launching, they used AI to write a compelling goal statement that aligned the internal team, the public, and all stakeholders on why they were asking and what success would look like.
 
 ### (2) Have you identified the right participants?
 
 The second step is determining who you need to hear from. Noveck distinguishes between "lived experience" and "credentialed expertise," arguing that both are valuable. Even before AI, offices of public engagement often relied on "usual suspects." AI can help map and identify participants who might otherwise be missed.
 
 ### (3) Can you reach the participants you identified?
 
 The third step is reaching people where they are. Gambrell emphasizes that outreach must be accessible in multiple senses: technical accessibility, language, format, channel, etc. Without targeted outreach to underrepresented communities, "we risk just hearing from the people whose perspectives are already represented."
 
 Example: [Bogotá, Colombia, deployed Chatico, an AI-powered WhatsApp chatbot for civic participation](https:/www.peoplepowered.org/news-content/digital-participation-case-study-bogota) . In participatory budgeting, the chatbot collected over 130,000 votes from more than 50,000 residents in just under two weeks, handling nearly 90% of digital votes. The largest digital participatory budgeting process ever recorded in Bogotá. Notably, 57% of participants were women, with strong representation from migrants and people with disabilities. Success factors included plain language and mobile-first design.
 
 AI application: AI can create multiple versions of outreach materials tailored to different audiences, translate content into multiple languages, and simplify technical jargon into plain language.
 
 ### 
 
 ### (4) Who is the right owner?
 
 The fourth step is determining who is responsible for each component of the engagement and, critically, for acting on community input. Gambrell notes that engagement projects are usually delivered by coalitions, so clear roles and responsibilities matter. When AI is used, project owners must also decide which tasks AI is and is not suitable for, and ensure ethical use. AI should be "on tap, not on top."
 
 Example: [California's wildfire recovery engagement brought together the state's Government Operations Agency, the Office of Data and Innovation, the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, the City of Los Angeles, the County of Los Angeles, and community organizations.](https:/carnegieendowment.org/posts/2025/09/engaged-california-la-wildfires-lessons?lang=en) The initiative is owned within the state government and championed by Governor Newsom. In its first phase, communities deliberated online using the [Ethelo platform](https:/ethelo.com) , generating more than 1,300 comments. Having responsible owners within government makes it more likely that community priorities will translate into implementable programs.
 
 ### 
 
 ### (5) Have you included incentives for participation?
 
 The fifth step addresses why people should participate. Incentives can be extrinsic (stipends, prizes, drawings) or intrinsic (civic duty, desire to do good). Gambrell also emphasizes reducing barriers through "wraparound services" like childcare, elder care, and transportation support. These show respect for the time, expertise, and experience people contribute.
 
 Northern Ireland's Voice Matters Initiative convenes an annual People's Panel (citizen assembly) in which residents deliberate on the community's future. Past topics have included mental health and creating a better future for young people. [This year, they began using Echo (from Dembrane), which uses AI to transcribe conversations, identify themes, and create visualizations in real time.](https:/www.peoplepowered.org/news-content/digital-participation-case-study-ireland) In contrast to past years, when facilitators spent multiple weekends manually comparing notes, insights are now reported back to participants at the end of each deliberation. Participants also receive stipends and childcare support.
 
 Real-time summaries and visualizations serve as intrinsic motivators by showing people their voices are heard. AI can also generate personalized thank-you notes or certificates of participation.
 
 ### 
 
 ### (6) Have you defined the tasks?
 
 The sixth step is to determine what you are asking participants to contribute and to provide clear instructions matched to their abilities. Gambrell emphasizes that if AI will be used for analysis later, you should collect responses in a format that supports that analysis. Speech-to-text capabilities can allow people who prefer talking to typing to contribute.
 
 Example: [Bowling Green, Kentucky, invited residents to share their vision for the community's future as part of long-term planning.](https:/medium.com/jigsaw/how-one-of-the-fastest-growing-cities-in-kentucky-used-ai-to-plan-for-the-next-25-years-3b70c4fd1412) The task was simple and clearly defined: respond to an open-ended prompt asking what you want your community's future to look like over the next 25 years. Participants could agree or disagree with others' submissions. Nearly 8,000 participants submitted nearly 4,000 ideas, with more than a million votes over one month. They used [Pol.is](http:/pol.is)
 
 for the deliberation platform and [Google Jigsaw's sense-making tool](https:/jigsaw-code.github.io/sensemaking-tools) to categorize ideas, identify agreement and disagreement, and produce an interactive report.
 
 ### 
 
 ### (7) Have you established the workflow?
 
 The seventh factor is having clear steps and project managing the engagement. Noveck argues for thinking beyond a single engagement to the whole policy-making process. Engagement can happen at multiple stages: defining the problem, generating solutions, implementing, and evaluating. "Part of our argument here is that what we can do is to think about how to use engagement... at every stage of the policy-making process."
 
 Example: [Vienna's climate team used Go Vocal (a platform used by 500+ cities) to collect ideas from residents for neighborhood sustainability projects.](https:/www.govocal.com/case-studies/vienna-climate-team-award-winning-hybrid-engagement-project) AI categorized more than a thousand submissions, detected overlaps, and surfaced emerging themes. City experts then evaluated the ideas for feasibility and, in collaboration with the original idea providers, refined them. Finally, a jury of randomly selected residents made final decisions on proposals. The multi-phase structure combined online and offline engagement, expert and citizen input.
 
 ### 
 
 ### (8) How will you evaluate inputs?
 
 The eighth factor is deciding in advance how you will evaluate the inputs you receive. Is this a popularity contest (sentiment) or a search for ideas (expertise)? Who will determine: credentialed experts, citizens, government insiders, or external reviewers? These criteria should be clear to your team and to the public.
 
 [Brazil's Senate allows residents to propose legislation. They are now using AI to bucket, cluster, group, and evaluate those submissions.](https:/rebootdemocracy.ai/blog/ai-lawmaking-brazil-senate-part-2)
 
 [In U.S. federal rulemaking, public comments that are relevant and insightful can affect the rule’s rationale and final design; the rule cannot be justified or repealed by tallying supportive versus opposing comments.](https:/uploads.federalregister.gov/uploads/2013/09/The-Rulemaking-Process.pdf)
 
 AI can categorize and assess input based on predefined criteria. "The clearer you tell people what the purpose of their submission is, the better they are going to participate," says Gambrell.
 
 ### 
 
 ### (9) How will you use what the group creates?
 
 The ninth factor is ensuring that participation leads to visible outcomes. Noveck states directly: "The number one reason people participate... is the notion that your participation matters, that it's relevant. The worst thing that we can do is to ask people, and then not listen to them." You do not have to accept every idea, but people must understand how their ideas will be used and feel heard.
 
 Cautionary example: During the Obama transition, Noveck's team solicited ideas for the first 100 days in office and received 125,000 submissions. "And you know what we did with those submissions? Nothing. Because we had no idea how we were gonna use them." The media opportunity was nice, but failing to act on input depresses trust in government.
 
 Positive example: [New Jersey's AI Task Force engagement led not just to a report but also to the implementation of public suggestions and specific policy commitments.](https:/rebootdemocracy.ai/blog/new-jersey-ai-task-force-policy-recommendations)
 
 ## 
 
 ## Takeaways for learners
 
 The checklist is a design tool. These nine factors emerged from reverse-engineering successful engagements. They represent the questions practitioners said they had to answer to run effective participation. Use them to audit and improve engagement design.
 
 Engagement fails most often at the beginning and end. Lack of clear purpose (Factor 1) and failure to close the loop (Factor 9) are recurring problems. The Obama transition example shows how even successful data collection can fail if there is no plan for use.
 
 Multi-phase engagement is newly practical. Before AI, analyzing engagement was slow, so engagement happened once. AI's speed in summarizing and categorizing makes it feasible to engage at multiple points in the policy cycle.
 
 Mobile-first, plain-language design reaches underrepresented groups. The Bogotá Chatico example shows that design choices (WhatsApp, plain language, workflow guidance) can dramatically change who participates. The 57% women participation rate is notable.
 
 Real-time feedback is an incentive. The Voice Matters example shows that AI-generated real-time summaries and visualizations help people feel heard immediately, rather than waiting weeks for manual analysis.
 
 ## 
 
 ## Audience notes
 
 ### 
 
 ### Reasons for attending:
 
 71% wanted to get familiar with new AI tools or technologies for engagement
 
 61% wanted to learn how to practice a new skill or technique
 
 45% wanted to increase confidence in using tools to facilitate public engagement
 
 42% wanted to build confidence in applying platforms to create public value
 
 ### Top challenges in online public engagement:
 
 42% cited lack of time or staff capacity
 
 39% cited limited technical skills or confidence with digital tools
 
 39% cited limited organizational support or leadership buy-in
 
 32% cited difficulty reaching diverse or representative audiences
 
 32% cited difficulty demonstrating the impact or value of engagement outcomes
 
 ### Participant locations and affiliations:
 
 New York (global coalition on armed conflict and education), New Jersey Office of Innovation, Sacramento (California High-Speed Rail Authority), Sweden, Honolulu, Portland (Portland State University doctoral research on public opinion in infrastructure planning), Tucson (Public Safety Communications), UNICEF Office of Innovation, Budapest (local ecosystem development), and others.
 
 ### 
 
 ### Questions raised in chat:
 
 “How do you prevent bots from skewing participatory processes?” (raised re: Bogotá)
 
 “Are there recommended AI models better suited for municipal government?”
 
 “Could participants dictate views while commuting or doing chores, with AI making remarks more coherent?”
 
 “How do you collect data with confidence that responses come from community members, not nefarious actors?”
 
 “Are there examples of AI engagement tools in school contexts for civic education?”
 
 Quotes
 
 ### Beth Simone Noveck (InnovateUS)
 
 "Citizen engagement, despite having fantastic technology, even before AI, we've had 30 years of the World Wide Web... and yet citizen engagement too often remains tokenistic, it remains occasional, or it remains very small."
 
 "We are not talking about getting faster by replacing engagement with AI. We are not talking about saying, look, you can just go ask ChatGPT instead of asking communities."
 
 "I have seen, in my experience, more often than not, people going out and doing engagement because they have to, not because they need to."
 
 "The number one reason people participate... is the notion that your participation matters, that it's relevant. The worst thing that we can do is to ask people, and then not listen to them."
 
 "We got 125,000 submissions. And you know what we did with those submissions? Nothing. Because we had no idea how we were gonna use them."
 
 "When I can rapidly summarize and draw insights from one phase, it can allow me then to do more forms of engagement."
 
 ### Dane Gambrell (The GovLab)
 
 "Without really targeted outreach and targeted outreach to diverse communities who are underrepresented in the existing decision-making processes, we risk just hearing from the people whose perspectives are already represented."
 
 "Responsible use is making sure that AI is on tap, not on top, that it's not being seen as a replacement, either for human decision making, or for real engagement with communities."
 
 "This is really transformative, because in contrast to past years where these deliberations would happen, and then facilitators would have to get together over this series of several weekends and compare notes and pull findings from the deliberations manually, now the AI transcription and summarization allows them to pull those insights in real time."
 
 ## 
 
 ## Platforms/Tools/Resources
 
 [All Our Ideas](https:/allourideas.org) — Open-source AI tool from Princeton and Citizens Foundation for idea generation and prioritization. Used in New Jersey AI Task Force. [https://allourideas.org](https:/allourideas.org)
 
 [Chatico (Bogotá) case study](https:/www.peoplepowered.org/news-content/digital-participation-case-study-bogota) — AI-powered WhatsApp chatbot for civic participation. Largest digital participatory budgeting in Bogotá history. WhatsApp number: (+57) 316 023 1524.
 
 [Ethello](https:/ethelo.com) — Deliberation platform with AI analysis. Used in California wildfire recovery engagement.
 
 [Dembrane](https:/www.dembrane.com/en-US/products/echo) — AI transcription and real-time visualization for in-person deliberations. [Used in Northern Ireland Voice Matters.](https:/www.peoplepowered.org/news-content/digital-participation-case-study-ireland)
 
 [Pol.is](http:/pol.is) — Platform for large-scale opinion gathering and clustering. Used in Bowling Green, Kentucky and vTaiwan.
 
 [Google Jigsaw Sensemaker](https:/jigsaw-code.github.io/sensemaking-tools) — AI tool for categorizing ideas and identifying areas of agreement/disagreement. Used in Bowling Green.
 
 [Go Vocal](https:/www.govocal.com) — Digital engagement platform used by 500+ cities. Used in Vienna climate engagement.
 
 [Reboot Democracy: Brazil Senate citizen participation](https:/rebootdemocracy.ai/blog/ai-lawmaking-brazil-senate) — Four ways citizens can participate in lawmaking, including submitting questions for hearings and proposing legislation.
 
 [New Jersey COVID science network](https:/fas.org/publication/do-you-have-covid-19-questions-we-have-answers-ask-a-scientist-launches) — 600 PhD scientists answering public health questions, in partnership with Federation of American Scientists.
 
 [Reboot Democracy: New Jersey AI Taskforce engagement](https:/rebootdemocracy.ai/blog/new-jersey-ai-task-force-policy-recommendations)
 
 [Bowling Green, Kentucky](https:/medium.com/jigsaw/how-one-of-the-fastest-growing-cities-in-kentucky-used-ai-to-plan-for-the-next-25-years-3b70c4fd1412) — 8,000 participants, 4,000 ideas, 1 million+ votes on 25-year community vision.
 
 [Vienna climate engagement](https:/www.govocal.com/case-studies/vienna-climate-team-award-winning-hybrid-engagement-project) — Multi-phase process with AI categorization, expert review, and citizen jury.
 
 [Digital Participation Platform Resource Center — People Powered](https:/www.peoplepowered.org/digital-participation)
 
 [Reboot Democracy: A-IEP project (AI tools built with communities)](https:/rebootdemocracy.ai/blog/when-communities-lead-appropriate-tech-and-change-follow)
